content: Glutamic acid and its salts, known as glutamates, are compounds that contribute to the umami or savory taste in food. Glutamic acid naturally occurs in many fermented or aged foods, such as soy sauce, fermented bean paste, and cheese, as well as in hydrolyzed protein products like yeast extract. In its sodium salt form, monosodium glutamate (MSG), it is widely used as a flavor enhancer in the food industry. When glutamic acid or its salts dissolve in water, they undergo a pH-dependent chemical equilibrium, forming various ionized states, including zwitterions. These ionized forms are collectively referred to as glutamates. The glutamate ion is the specific form responsible for the umami taste, regardless of the initial form of glutamic acid added. However, crystalline salts like MSG dissolve more readily and quickly than crystalline glutamic acid, making them more effective as flavor enhancers. The flavor-enhancing properties of glutamic acid and other amino acids were scientifically identified in the early 20th century, although the compound itself was first discovered in 1866 by German chemist Karl Heinrich Leopold Ritthausen. In 1907, Japanese researcher Kikunae Ikeda identified glutamic acid as the source of the unique savory flavor in kombu broth, which he termed umami. He later patented a method to mass-produce MSG, a crystalline salt of glutamic acid. Only the L-glutamate enantiomer has flavor-enhancing properties. Commercially produced MSG contains over 99.6% of the naturally predominant L-glutamate form, which is a higher proportion than the free glutamate ions found in naturally occurring foods. Fermented products like soy sauce and Worcestershire sauce contain comparable levels of glutamate to foods with added MSG, but the glutamate in these products may include up to 5% of the D-enantiomer. Glutamic acid activates specific receptors in taste buds, such as the T1R1/T1R3 amino acid receptor and metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR4 and mGluR1), to produce the umami taste. Umami is one of the five basic tastes and is often described as savory or meaty. Glutamate is a ubiquitous amino acid found in all living cells, primarily in its bound form as part of proteins. Only free glutamate, however, can enhance food flavor. Foods like tomatoes, fermented soy products, yeast extracts, sharp cheeses, and hydrolyzed protein products owe part of their flavor-enhancing properties to free glutamate ions. Traditional Asian cuisine used natural seaweed broths, such as kelp, to enhance umami flavors in soups. Modern manufacturers, such as Ajinomoto, use strains of Micrococcus glutamicus bacteria to produce glutamic acid, which is then processed into MSG. Hydrolyzed proteins, created by acid or enzymatic treatment of proteins, contain free amino acids, including glutamate, at concentrations of 5% to 20%. These hydrolyzed proteins, such as yeast extract, are used in foods like canned vegetables, soups, and processed meats in a manner similar to MSG. In 1968, Dr. Ho Man Kwok described a set of symptoms, including numbness, weakness, and palpitations, after consuming Chinese food, coining the term Chinese restaurant syndrome. This sparked widespread concern about MSG. However, scientific research has not substantiated claims that MSG affects a significant portion of the population. The FDA classified MSG as generally recognized as safe (GRAS) in 1959, and subsequent reviews by organizations like the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) and the World Health Organization have reaffirmed its safety. While some individuals may experience mild, transient symptoms after consuming MSG, these reactions are not considered a significant health risk. Glutamate is absorbed rapidly in the gastrointestinal tract, potentially causing spikes in plasma glutamate levels. Glutamic acid belongs to a class of chemicals known as excitotoxins, which, at high levels, have been shown in animal studies to cause neurotoxicity in areas of the brain unprotected by the blood-brain barrier. The relevance of these findings to humans remains debated. Some researchers argue that humans are less susceptible to excitotoxicity than rodents, while others suggest that humans may be more vulnerable, particularly infants and young children. Typical dietary levels of MSG are not believed to cause harmful plasma glutamate spikes in adults, but concerns persist about potential long-term effects. Animal studies have shown that MSG can indirectly contribute to obesity by disrupting hypothalamic appetite regulation, leading to increased food intake. However, some studies suggest that this effect is not solely dependent on increased food consumption. Epidemiological studies in humans have not consistently linked MSG consumption to obesity, and no significant effects on blood sugar or cholesterol levels have been observed. In the United States, the FDA requires MSG to be explicitly listed on food labels. However, free glutamate may also be present in other additives, such as hydrolyzed vegetable proteins, yeast extracts, and soy extracts, which are not always labeled as containing MSG. The FDA has proposed additional labeling requirements to clarify the presence of glutamate in such products. In Europe, MSG is designated as E621, and in Australia and New Zealand, it must be labeled with its additive class name and either its name or International Numbering System (INS) code (621).
